q: "Unlike his talkative brother, Bilal was reticent and rarely shared his opinions in class." In this sentence, 'reticent' most nearly means:
x: The contrast clue 'unlike his talkative brother' and the phrase 'rarely shared his opinions' show that reticent means reserved, not inclined to speak. Nothing in the sentence suggests rudeness or carelessness.

q: "The fame of most social media stars is ephemeral; a video that is popular on Monday is forgotten by Friday." The word 'ephemeral' means:
x: The clause after the semicolon explains the word: popular on Monday, forgotten by Friday. So ephemeral means lasting a very short time. Permanent is the opposite.

q: "Fatima was so meticulous that she checked every figure in the report three times before submitting it." The word 'meticulous' means:
x: Checking every figure three times is the example clue: meticulous means showing great care about small details. Nothing in the sentence shows speed, worry or pride.

q: "Living on a small pension, Hamza's grandfather was frugal: he mended his old shoes rather than buy new ones and never wasted food." 'Frugal' means:
x: The examples after the colon (mending old shoes, never wasting food) show that frugal means careful and economical in spending. Greedy, careless and generous do not fit these examples.

q: "The instructions were so ambiguous that half the students answered one question and half answered another." The word 'ambiguous' means:
o: Open to more than one meaning
x: Students understood the same instructions in two different ways, which is the clue that ambiguous means having more than one possible meaning. Length or falseness would not explain the split.

q: "The once-busy telegraph office now stands empty; the service became obsolete after mobile phones arrived." 'Obsolete' means:
x: The office 'now stands empty' because a newer technology replaced it, so obsolete means out of date and no longer used. Very popular is the opposite of what the clue shows.

q: "After the long journey, Ayesha felt so lethargic that she could barely lift her school bag, let alone run for the bus." 'Lethargic' means:
x: Being barely able to lift a bag, let alone run, shows a lack of energy, so lethargic means sluggish and tired. Excited and restless is the opposite; calm does not explain the weakness.

q: "Mobile phones have become ubiquitous; you see them in villages, classrooms, hospitals and even at funerals." The word 'ubiquitous' means:
x: The list of very different places where phones are seen is the example clue: ubiquitous means present everywhere. The sentence says nothing about cost, usefulness or newness.

q: "The witness gave such a lucid account of the accident that the police had no difficulty understanding exactly what had happened." 'Lucid' means:
x: The result clause 'no difficulty understanding' shows that a lucid account is clear and easily understood. A brief, incomplete account would have caused difficulty.

q: "Planting trees along the roads can mitigate the heat of summer, making the streets a few degrees cooler." The word 'mitigate' means:
x: The phrase 'making the streets a few degrees cooler' shows the heat is reduced, so mitigate means make less severe. Increase is the opposite meaning.

q: "Far from being indolent, the new clerk arrived early, worked through lunch and was the last to leave." The word 'indolent' means:
x: 'Far from being' signals a contrast: the clerk's behaviour is the opposite of indolent. Since he is hardworking, indolent must mean lazy. Hardworking is the trap, because it describes the clerk, not the word.

q: "The obsequious waiter bowed every few seconds, agreed with everything the rich guest said and laughed loudly at all his jokes." 'Obsequious' means:
x: Constant bowing, agreeing with everything and laughing at every joke all show excessive eagerness to please someone important. That is the meaning of obsequious; the other options contradict the examples.

q: "The old man was too feeble to climb the stairs without help." The closest synonym of 'feeble' is:
x: Feeble means lacking physical strength, i.e. weak; that is why he needs help on the stairs. Lazy suggests unwillingness, not inability.

q: Which word gives a POSITIVE description of a person who does not change his mind easily?
x: All four words describe someone who holds firmly to a decision, but only 'determined' praises this quality. Stubborn, obstinate and pig-headed carry a negative shade of unreasonable refusal to change.

q: Choose the word that best fits: "The little boy ___ secretly through the gap in the curtain to see who was at the door."
x: To peep is to look quickly and secretly through a small opening, which matches 'secretly through the gap'. Stare and gaze suggest long open looking, and glare suggests anger.

q: Choose the word that best fits: "Exhausted and dizzy after the race, the runner ___ towards the finish line, almost falling twice."
x: To stagger is to walk unsteadily, as if about to fall, which fits 'exhausted and dizzy' and 'almost falling'. Strolled is relaxed, while marched and strode are firm and confident.

q: Choose the word that best fits: "The gang leader was ___ throughout the district for his cruelty."
x: All four words mean 'well known', but notorious means famous for something bad, which suits cruelty. Renowned, celebrated and distinguished are used for admirable fame.

q: Choose the word that best fits: "Even at eighty, Nani has a ___ sense of wonder, delighting in every bird and flower she sees."
x: Childlike has a positive shade: innocent and fresh like a child, which matches 'delighting in every bird'. Childish, immature and infantile are negative, suggesting silly behaviour.

q: Ali left his umbrella at home on the rainiest day of the year. Soaked, he said, "Well, that was a brilliant decision." Here 'brilliant' is used to mean:
x: Ali is speaking ironically: he says the opposite of what he means. A decision that left him soaked was foolish, so 'brilliant' here means foolish, not clever.

q: A writer says: "Our 'luxury hotel' turned out to have broken beds and no running water." By putting 'luxury hotel' in quotation marks, the writer is:
o: Mocking the claim made about the hotel
x: The quotation marks are ironic: broken beds and no water show the hotel was anything but luxurious. The writer is mocking the description, not praising or recommending it.

q: A newspaper column says: "Our city's roads now have so many potholes that residents use them as free swimming pools in the monsoon." The writer's main aim is to:
o: Praise the city for saving money
Criticise the poor roads through mockery
x: This is satire: an exaggerated, humorous picture used to criticise something, here the neglected roads. Nobody really uses potholes as pools, so the aim is not to advertise or advise.

q: Hamza rewrites a serious patriotic poem line by line, keeping its rhythm but making it about his love for biryani, to make his friends laugh. His poem is a:
x: A parody imitates the style of a serious work for comic effect, exactly what Hamza does. An elegy mourns the dead, a eulogy praises someone, and a ballad tells a story in song-like verse.

q: In which sentence is the word 'generous' used ironically?
o: The generous donor paid for the whole new hospital ward.
The landlord was so generous that he raised the rent three times in one year.
She served a generous portion of rice to each guest.
Thanks to a generous scholarship, Bilal could study abroad.
x: Raising the rent three times is the opposite of generosity, so calling the landlord generous is ironic: the writer means he is greedy. In the other sentences generous is used in its normal, literal sense.

q: Which pair shows a word with a positive shade of meaning followed by a synonym with a negative shade?
x: Confident (positive) and arrogant (negative) both describe self-belief, in that order. The reversed pair has the order wrong, confident and self-assured are both positive, and arrogant and boastful are both negative.

q: Choose the correct pronoun: "Ayesha and Sara finished ___ homework before dinner."
x: Two nouns joined by 'and' form a plural antecedent, so the plural possessive 'their' is needed. 'They're' means 'they are' and is not a possessive.

q: Choose the correct word: "The old tree has lost most of ___ leaves."
x: The antecedent 'tree' is singular and not a person, so the possessive is 'its'. 'It's' is the short form of 'it is' or 'it has'.

q: Choose the correct pronoun: "Neither the principal nor the teachers had brought ___ umbrellas."
x: With 'neither ... nor', the pronoun agrees with the nearer antecedent. The nearer one, 'teachers', is plural, so 'their' is correct.

q: Choose the correct pronoun: "The children dressed ___ quickly for school."
x: The reflexive pronoun must agree with the plural antecedent 'children', so 'themselves' is correct. 'Theirselves' is not standard English, and 'himself' is singular.

q: Choose the correct relative pronoun: "The machine ___ makes the ice has broken down."
x: The antecedent 'machine' is a thing, and the relative pronoun is the subject of 'makes', so 'which' is correct. 'Who' and 'whom' refer to people.

q: Find the error: "The students thanked their teacher, who had helped him prepare for the exam."
x: The pronoun refers back to 'the students', which is plural, so 'him' should be 'them'. 'Their' correctly agrees with 'students', and 'who' correctly refers to the teacher.

q: Which sentence keeps the pronoun in agreement with its antecedent?
o: If students revise daily, you will remember more.
If students revise daily, he will remember more.
If students revise daily, it will remember more.
If students revise daily, they will remember more.
x: The antecedent 'students' is third person plural, so the pronoun must be 'they'. 'You' wrongly shifts the person, and 'he' and 'it' are singular.

q: Choose the correct pronoun: "Many of the passengers had lost ___ luggage when the bus overturned."
x: 'Many' is always plural, so the pronoun referring to 'many of the passengers' must be the plural 'their'. 'Its' would wrongly point to the bus.

q: In which sentence does the pronoun have one clear antecedent?
o: Bilal lost his wallet, but he found it later in the car.
When Ali met Hamza, he was very tired.
Sara told Ayesha that she had won the prize.
The book fell off the shelf, and it broke.
x: Only Bilal can be 'he' and only the wallet can be 'it', so the reference is clear. In the others the pronoun could refer to either of two nouns: Ali or Hamza, Sara or Ayesha, the book or the shelf.

q: Choose the correct word: "The old house, ___ roof had collapsed in the storm, was finally pulled down."
x: 'Whose' is the possessive relative pronoun and can refer to things as well as people: the roof belongs to the house. 'Who's' means 'who is', and 'which roof' or 'where roof' do not make grammatical clauses here.

q: Choose the correct pronoun: "This bag isn't Ali's; ___ is the blue one near the door."
x: The pronoun stands for 'Ali's bag', so the possessive pronoun 'his' is needed as the subject of 'is'. 'Him' and 'himself' are object forms, and 'he' does not show possession.

q: Choose the correct pronoun: "My sisters and I packed ___ own lunch boxes."
x: An antecedent that includes 'I' is first person plural, so the possessive adjective is 'our'. 'Their' would leave out the speaker, and 'ours' cannot stand before a noun.

q: Choose the correct tense: "While Sara ___ dinner, the lights suddenly went out."
x: The past continuous 'was cooking' shows an action in progress that was interrupted by a shorter past action ('the lights went out'). 'Had been cooked' is passive and makes no sense with Sara as subject.

q: Choose the correct verb: "I ___ my house keys yesterday."
x: 'Yesterday' names a finished past time, so the simple past 'lost' is needed. The present perfect cannot be used with a finished past time expression.

q: Choose the correct verb: "By the time the ambulance arrived, the injured man ___ consciousness."
x: Of two past events, the one that happened first takes the past perfect. He lost consciousness before the ambulance arrived, so 'had lost' is correct.

q: Choose the correct verb: "If it rains tomorrow, the cricket match ___."
x: This is a first conditional about a real future possibility: 'if' + present simple, then 'will' + verb. 'Would be' belongs to the second conditional and 'would have been' to the third.

q: Choose the correct verb: "If I ___ a bird, I would fly over the mountains."
x: An imaginary present situation takes the second conditional: 'if' + past form, then 'would' + verb. 'Were' is used here; 'am' and 'will be' belong to real conditions, and 'had been' to the third conditional.

q: Choose the correct verb: "If Hamza had left home earlier, he ___ the train."
x: 'If' + past perfect is the third conditional, about an unreal past. Its result clause uses 'would have' + past participle: 'would have caught'.

q: Choose the correct verb: "Our physics teacher told us that light ___ faster than sound."
x: A universal truth stays in the present simple even after a past reporting verb, so 'travels' is correct. The other forms would wrongly make a permanent fact sound like a past or temporary event.

q: Choose the correct verb: "I will phone you as soon as I ___ home."
x: In a time clause beginning with 'as soon as', 'when', 'before' or 'after', the present simple is used for a future action. 'Will reach' is a common error here.

q: Choose the correct verb: "Fatima and I ___ each other since we were in primary school."
x: An action or state that began in the past and continues now, with 'since', takes the present perfect: 'have known'. 'Know' is a state verb and is not used in the continuous form.

q: Which sentence uses the tense correctly with 'last week'?
o: I have seen that film last week.
I saw that film last week.
I have saw that film last week.
I was seen that film last week.
x: 'Last week' is a finished past time, so the simple past 'saw' is correct. The present perfect cannot take a finished time expression, 'have saw' uses the wrong verb form, and 'was seen' is passive.

q: Choose the correct verb: "If he ___ the doctor's warning yesterday, he would not be in hospital now."
x: This is a mixed conditional: the condition is about the past ('yesterday'), so it needs the past perfect 'had heeded', while the result ('now') uses 'would' + verb. 'Heeded' would refer to the present, which clashes with 'yesterday'.

q: Choose the correct verb: "It is already eight o'clock; it is high time we ___ for the station."
x: After 'It is high time' + subject, the past simple is used even though the meaning is present or future. So 'it is high time we left' is correct, not the present or future form.

q: Choose the correct form: "The teacher made the students ___ the essay again."
x: In the active voice, 'make' + object is followed by the bare infinitive (without 'to'): 'made the students write'. 'Made them to write' is a common error.

q: Choose the correct form: "Hamza went to the bank ___ some money."
x: The infinitive 'to withdraw' shows the purpose of his going to the bank. The finite forms 'withdraws' and 'withdrew' cannot follow here without a conjunction.

q: Choose the correct form: "The box was too heavy for Sara ___."
x: The pattern 'too + adjective + (for someone) + to-infinitive' shows that something is not possible: 'too heavy for Sara to lift'.

q: In the sentence "To swim across the river was Bilal's dream", the infinitive phrase 'To swim across the river' acts as the:
x: The infinitive phrase tells us what 'was Bilal's dream', so it is the subject of the verb 'was'. 'Bilal's dream' is the complement, not the subject.

q: In "Fatima has a lot of homework to finish tonight", the infinitive phrase 'to finish tonight' works as:
x: The phrase tells us which homework, or what kind: homework to finish tonight. So it works like an adjective qualifying the noun 'homework'. The object of 'has' is 'a lot of homework'.

q: Choose the correct form: "My father allowed me ___ the car to college."
x: 'Allow' + object is followed by the to-infinitive: 'allowed me to drive'. Unlike 'make' and 'let', it does not take the bare infinitive.

q: Choose the correct form: "The thief seems ___ through the back window last night."
x: The seeming is now but the escape happened earlier ('last night'), so the perfect infinitive 'to have escaped' is needed. 'To escape' would refer to the present or future.

q: Choose the correct form: "The boy was made ___ for his rude remark."
x: In the active voice 'make' takes the bare infinitive (they made him apologise), but in the passive voice 'to' returns: 'he was made to apologise'. Students often wrongly carry the bare infinitive into the passive.

q: Choose the correct form: "You had better ___ a doctor about that cough."
x: 'Had better' is followed by the bare infinitive without 'to': 'had better see'. 'Had better to see' is incorrect.

q: Choose the correct form: "Ali is now old enough ___ his own decisions."
x: The pattern 'adjective + enough + to-infinitive' shows that someone has the required quality: 'old enough to make'. The gerund and bare forms are not used after 'enough' here.

q: In which sentence is the infinitive phrase the object of the verb?
o: Ayesha wants to become a surgeon.
Ayesha studies hard to become a surgeon.
Ayesha's aim is to become a surgeon.
Ayesha is the first girl in her family to become a surgeon.
x: In 'wants to become a surgeon' the phrase answers 'wants what?', so it is the object. In the others it shows purpose (adverb), completes 'is' (complement), or describes 'girl' (adjective).

q: In which sentence is 'to' a preposition and NOT part of an infinitive?
o: Bilal hopes to meet his cousins.
Bilal decided to meet his cousins.
Bilal is looking forward to meeting his cousins.
Bilal was happy to meet his cousins.
x: In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, which is why it is followed by the gerund 'meeting'. In the other sentences 'to meet' is an infinitive.

q: Choose the correct form: "Sara enjoys ___ novels in her free time."
x: The verb 'enjoy' is followed by a gerund, not an infinitive: 'enjoys reading'. 'Enjoys to read' is a common error.

q: Choose the correct form: "___ every morning keeps Grandfather fit and cheerful."
x: The subject of 'keeps' must be a noun form; the gerund 'Walking' works as a noun. The other forms are verbs and cannot be the subject here.

q: Choose the correct form: "The suspect denied ___ the shop window."
x: 'Deny' is followed by a gerund: 'denied breaking'. It does not take a to-infinitive, and 'to have broke' also uses the wrong past participle.

q: Choose the correct form: "After much thought, Bilal has decided ___ medicine at university."
x: Unlike 'enjoy' or 'avoid', the verb 'decide' is followed by the to-infinitive: 'decided to study'. 'Decided studying' is incorrect.

q: Choose the correct form: "I am looking forward to ___ you at the wedding."
x: In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, and a preposition is followed by a gerund: 'looking forward to seeing'.

q: Choose the correct form: "On the way home, Ali stopped ___ some bread, so he reached home late."
x: 'Stop' + to-infinitive means stopping one activity in order to do another, here to buy bread on the way. 'Stopped buying' would mean he gave up the habit of buying bread, which does not fit.

q: Choose the correct form: "I clearly remember ___ the door when I left, but now it is open!"
x: 'Remember' + gerund refers to a memory of something already done in the past. 'Remember to lock' would mean not forgetting a duty still to be done, which does not fit 'when I left'.

q: In the sentence "Hamza is fond of playing cricket", the gerund phrase 'playing cricket' is the:
x: The gerund phrase comes after the preposition 'of' and completes it, so it is the object of the preposition. The subject is 'Hamza', and 'is' does not take an object.

q: In which sentence is the -ing word a gerund?
o: Swimming is good exercise for the whole body.
The swimming boy waved to us from the lake.
The boy is swimming in the lake.
Swimming across the lake, the boy saw a fish.
x: A gerund works as a noun; here 'Swimming' is the subject of 'is'. In the others the -ing word is a participle: an adjective ('swimming boy'), part of a continuous verb ('is swimming'), or a participle phrase describing the boy.

q: Choose the correct form: "Would you mind ___ the window? It is very hot in here."
x: 'Mind' is followed by a gerund: 'Would you mind opening'. It does not take a to-infinitive.

q: Choose the correct form: "My grandfather is not used to ___ in such cold weather."
x: In 'be used to' (meaning 'be accustomed to'), 'to' is a preposition and takes a gerund: 'is not used to living'. Do not confuse it with 'used to live', which describes a past habit.

q: Find the error: "The doctor advised him to avoid to eat oily food."
x: 'Avoid' is followed by a gerund, so 'to eat' should be 'eating': 'to avoid eating oily food'. 'Advised him to avoid' is correct, because 'advise' + object takes the to-infinitive.

q: Which sentence places the adverb of frequency 'always' correctly?
o: Ali comes always to school on time.
Ali comes to always school on time.
Ali always to school comes on time.
Ali always comes to school on time.
x: An adverb of frequency normally goes before the main verb: 'always comes'. It does not come between a verb and its following phrase.

q: Which sentence places 'never' correctly with the verb 'be'?
o: Sara is late for never her lessons.
Never Sara is late for her lessons.
Sara is late never for her lessons.
Sara is never late for her lessons.
x: With the verb 'be', an adverb of frequency comes after it: 'is never late'. Putting 'never' first would require inversion, and it cannot go inside the phrase 'for her lessons'.

q: Which sentence places 'never' correctly in a verb with an auxiliary?
o: My uncle has never visited Karachi.
My uncle has visited never Karachi.
My uncle has visited Karachi never.
Never my uncle has visited Karachi.
x: With an auxiliary, an adverb of frequency goes between the auxiliary and the main verb: 'has never visited'. If 'never' is moved to the front, the auxiliary must come before the subject ('Never has my uncle...').

q: Which sentence places the adverb of manner correctly?
x: An adverb of manner usually comes after the verb and its object, and must not separate a verb from its object: 'speaks English fluently'. 'Fluent' is an adjective, not an adverb.

q: Which sentence means that nobody other than Bilal passed the test?
x: 'Only' limits the word it is placed next to. Before 'Bilal' it means no one else passed. Before 'passed' it means he merely passed (did not do better), and before or after 'the test' it limits what he passed.

q: Which sentence clearly means that fruit is the one thing Hamza eats at night?
o: At night, Hamza eats only fruit.
Only Hamza eats fruit at night.
Hamza eats fruit only at night.
Hamza eats fruit at night only.
x: 'Only fruit' limits what he eats at night. 'Only Hamza' means nobody else eats fruit at night, while 'only at night' and 'at night only' limit the time he eats fruit, not the food.

q: The puzzle was so easy that Fatima's six-year-old brother could solve it. Which sentence shows this meaning?
o: Her six-year-old brother solved even the puzzle.
Even her six-year-old brother solved the puzzle.
Her even six-year-old brother solved the puzzle.
Her six-year-old brother solved the puzzle, even.
x: 'Even' stresses the word it is placed next to. Before 'her six-year-old brother' it shows that the most unlikely person solved it, so the puzzle was easy. 'Even the puzzle' suggests the puzzle was the hardest task; 'her even six-year-old brother' puts it in the wrong place altogether.

q: Which sentence puts the adverbs of manner, place and time in the correct order?
o: The children happily in the park played yesterday.
The children played happily in the park yesterday.
Yesterday happily the children played in the park.
The children played in yesterday the park happily.
x: When several adverbs come after the verb, the usual order is manner, place, time: 'happily (how) in the park (where) yesterday (when)'. The other sentences break up the verb phrase or the phrase 'in the park'.

q: Choose the correct words: "Is the water ___ for a bath?"
x: As an adverb, 'enough' comes after the adjective or adverb it modifies: 'warm enough'. 'Enoughly' is not an English word.

q: Which sentence correctly begins with the negative adverb 'Never'?
o: Never have I seen such a beautiful sunset.
Never I have seen such a beautiful sunset.
Never I saw such a beautiful sunset.
Never have I saw such a beautiful sunset.
x: When a negative adverb such as 'never' or 'seldom' begins a sentence for emphasis, the auxiliary comes before the subject: 'Never have I seen'. 'Have I saw' also uses the wrong verb form.

q: In the sentence "The guests will arrive soon", the word 'soon' is an adverb of:
x: 'Soon' answers the question 'when?', so it is an adverb of time. Adverbs of time like this usually come at the end of the clause.

q: Choose the correct preposition: "The meeting will begin ___ nine o'clock."
x: 'At' is used for an exact clock time: 'at nine o'clock'. 'On' is for days and dates, and 'in' for months, years and longer periods.

q: Choose the correct preposition: "Pakistan became independent ___ 1947."
x: 'In' is used with years, months and seasons: 'in 1947'. 'On' would be used with a full date such as 14 August 1947.

q: Choose the correct preposition: "After the winter holidays, our school reopens ___ Monday."
x: Days of the week and dates take 'on': 'on Monday'. 'In' is for months and years, and 'at' for clock times.

q: Choose the correct preposition: "Hamza has been waiting at the clinic ___ two hours."
x: 'For' is used with a length of time ('two hours'), while 'since' is used with a starting point ('since ten o'clock'). Both go with the present perfect.

q: Choose the correct preposition: "Fatima has been ill ___ last Friday."
x: 'Last Friday' is a point in time when the illness began, and the present perfect shows it continues, so 'since' is correct. 'For' needs a length of time, such as 'for three days'.

q: Which sentence means that Sara was already inside the garden and was walking about there?
o: Sara was walking into the garden.
Sara was walking onto the garden.
Sara was walking towards the garden.
Sara was walking in the garden.
x: 'In' shows position inside a place, so 'walking in the garden' means moving about within it. 'Into' shows movement from outside to inside, and 'towards' shows direction without arrival.

q: Choose the correct preposition: "A sparrow flew ___ the open window and landed on my desk."
x: 'Through' shows movement from one side of an opening to the other, so the bird came in by the window and reached the desk. 'Across', 'along' and 'over' would not bring it inside the room.

q: Choose the correct preposition: "The children waved as the train moved slowly ___ the station, getting closer every second."
x: 'Towards' shows movement in the direction of a place, which matches 'getting closer'. 'From' and 'beyond' show movement away from or past it.

q: Choose the correct preposition: "Hamza looked both ways and then walked ___ the road, from one side to the other."
x: 'Across' means from one side of a surface to the other side, which matches 'from one side to the other'. 'Along' means following its length, and 'through' is used for passing within something enclosed, like a tunnel.

q: Choose the correct preposition: "The owl hunts ___ night and sleeps during the day."
x: 'Night' takes 'at' in the fixed phrase 'at night', although we say 'in the morning' and 'in the evening'. 'On' is for days and dates.

q: Choose the correct preposition: "Hurry up! The train will leave ___ ten minutes."
x: 'In' + a period of time shows when something will happen, counting from now: 'in ten minutes'. 'Since' needs a past starting point, and 'at' needs an exact time.

q: Choose the correct pair: "Our cousins arrived ___ Lahore late ___ night."
x: 'Arrive in' is used with cities and countries ('arrived in Lahore'), and 'night' takes 'at' ('late at night'). The pairs with 'at Lahore', 'on Lahore' or 'in night' each break one of these rules.

q: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: "Ali studied hard for the test; ___, he failed to pass it."
x: The second clause is the opposite of what we expect from the first, so a contrast word is needed. "Therefore" would wrongly make failing the result of studying.

q: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: "The roads were flooded. ___, the schools remained closed for two days."
x: The closing of schools is the result of the flooding, so a cause-and-effect word fits. "Nevertheless" would signal an unexpected outcome, which this is not.

q: Choose the correct option: "___ the heavy rain, the match started on time."
x: "Despite" is followed by a noun phrase ("the heavy rain") and shows contrast. "Although" needs a full clause with a verb, such as "Although it rained heavily".

q: Choose the correct option: "___ she was tired, Ayesha finished her assignment before midnight."
x: A full clause ("she was tired") follows the gap, so the conjunction "although" is needed. "Despite" and "in spite of" must be followed by a noun or gerund, not a clause.

q: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: "Smoking damages the lungs; ___, it raises the risk of heart disease."
x: The second clause adds a further harmful effect of smoking, so an addition word ("moreover") is needed. "However" and "nonetheless" signal contrast, which is not present.

q: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: "You must submit the form by Friday; ___, your admission will be cancelled."
x: "Otherwise" means "if you do not do this", which links the deadline to its consequence. "Hence" would wrongly say that submitting the form causes the cancellation.

q: In which sentence is the transitional word used logically?
o: Hamza was ill; however, he stayed at home.
Hamza was ill; for instance, he stayed at home.
Hamza was ill; in contrast, he stayed at home.
Hamza was ill; therefore, he stayed at home.
x: Staying at home is a result of being ill, so "therefore" fits. "However" and "in contrast" wrongly suggest the two ideas oppose each other.

q: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
o: Although the bus was late, but we arrived on time.
Despite of the delay, we arrived on time.
In spite the bus was late, we arrived on time.
Even though the bus was late, we arrived on time.
x: "Even though" correctly introduces a contrasting clause. "Although" must not be paired with "but", "despite" never takes "of", and "in spite" needs "of" plus a noun.

q: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: "Fatima wanted to become a doctor; ___, she chose biology in FSc."
x: Choosing biology follows naturally from her aim, so "accordingly" (meaning "for that reason") fits. "Nevertheless" would wrongly signal an unexpected choice.

q: Choose the phrase that best completes the sentence: "Some fruits are rich in vitamin C, ___ oranges and guavas."
x: Oranges and guavas are examples of fruits rich in vitamin C, so "for example" fits. The other words show result or contrast, which make no sense here.

q: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: "The first group of volunteers rested; ___, the second group ran for twenty minutes."
x: "Meanwhile" shows that the two actions happened at the same time. The second group running is neither a result of nor an example of the first group resting.

q: Choose the phrase that best completes the sentence: "Hamza is not lazy; ___, he is the most hard-working boy in the class."
x: "On the contrary" is used after a negative statement to introduce the opposite, stronger truth. "In addition" would add a further point, but being hard-working replaces the idea of laziness rather than adding to it.

q: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence.
o: It's raining, and the dog has hurt its paw.
Its raining, and the dog has hurt it's paw.
It's raining, and the dog has hurt it's paw.
Its raining, and the dog has hurt its paw.
x: "It's" is the short form of "it is", so it is needed in "It's raining". The possessive "its" (belonging to it) never takes an apostrophe.

q: Which sentence ends with the correct punctuation mark?
x: A direct question ends with a question mark, and no comma is needed inside this short question.

q: Which sentence correctly joins two complete clauses?
o: The lecture ended late, the students missed the bus.
The lecture ended late; and the students missed the bus.
The lecture ended late; the students missed the bus.
The lecture; ended late the students missed the bus.
x: A semicolon can join two complete, closely related clauses without a conjunction. Joining them with only a comma is a comma splice, and a semicolon is not used before "and" here.

q: Which sentence correctly introduces a list?
o: Bring three things; a pen, a ruler and an eraser.
Bring: three things a pen, a ruler and an eraser.
Bring three things: a pen, a ruler and an eraser.
Bring three things, a pen: a ruler and an eraser.
x: A colon introduces a list after a complete clause ("Bring three things"). A semicolon cannot introduce a list, and a colon must not split a verb from its object.

q: Which sentence correctly punctuates the spoken words?
x: The exact words spoken are enclosed in a pair of quotation marks, with a comma after "said". There is no comma between a subject and its verb.

q: Choose the correct form: "The two ___ results were announced together."
x: For a plural noun ending in -s, the possessive is formed by adding only an apostrophe: "brothers'". "Brother's" refers to one brother, which contradicts "two".

q: Which sentence uses commas correctly around the relative clause?
o: My mother who teaches chemistry, wakes up early.
My mother, who teaches chemistry wakes up early.
My mother, who teaches chemistry, wakes up early.
My mother who, teaches chemistry, wakes up early.
x: A person has only one mother, so "who teaches chemistry" is extra (non-defining) information and must be enclosed by a pair of commas.

q: Choose the correctly written form: "We ___ finished the work yet."
x: In a contraction the apostrophe replaces the missing letter: "have not" becomes "haven't", with the apostrophe where the "o" of "not" was.

q: Which sentence correctly punctuates a list of names with titles?
o: The meeting was attended by: Ali; the principal, Sara; the head teacher, and Bilal; the clerk.
The meeting was attended by Ali the principal; Sara, the head teacher, and; Bilal the clerk.
The meeting was attended by Ali, the principal; Sara, the head teacher; and Bilal, the clerk.
The meeting was attended by Ali, the principal, Sara; the head teacher, Bilal; and the clerk.
x: When the items of a list already contain commas, semicolons separate the items. Each name stays joined to its title by a comma, so the reader can see there are three people.

q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly as an exclamation?
o: What a beautiful view this is?
What a beautiful view, this is!
What a beautiful view this is!
What, a beautiful view this is.
x: A sentence beginning "What a..." that expresses strong feeling is an exclamation and ends with an exclamation mark, not a question mark.

q: Which sentence correctly punctuates the quoted question?
x: The question mark belongs to the quoted question, so it goes inside the quotation marks, and no extra full stop is added after it. The quoted sentence begins with a capital letter.

q: Which sentence has all its commas in the right places?
o: However the results, which surprised everyone were never published.
However, the results which surprised everyone, were never published.
However, the results, which surprised everyone were never published.
However, the results, which surprised everyone, were never published.
x: An opening "However" is followed by a comma, and the non-defining clause "which surprised everyone" needs a comma on both sides. Each wrong sentence leaves out one of these commas.

q: What kind of sentence is "Please close the door."?
x: An imperative sentence gives a command or makes a request. A declarative sentence makes a statement, and an interrogative sentence asks a question.

q: "Ali went to the market, and Sara stayed at home." This sentence is
x: It has two independent clauses joined by the coordinating conjunction "and", and no dependent clause, so it is a compound sentence.

q: "When the bell rang, the students left the room." This sentence is
x: It has one independent clause ("the students left the room") and one dependent clause ("When the bell rang"), which makes it complex.

q: In "The boy with the red cap is my cousin", the phrase "with the red cap" is
x: The phrase describes the noun "boy" (which boy?), so it does the work of an adjective. It has no subject and verb of its own, so it is not a clause.

q: In "She spoke in a gentle voice", the phrase "in a gentle voice" is
x: The phrase tells how she spoke, so it modifies the verb "spoke" and works as an adverb. It has no finite verb, so it cannot be a clause.

q: In "To win the gold medal was her dream", the words "To win the gold medal" function as
o: a noun phrase acting as the subject
a dependent clause with its own subject
x: The infinitive phrase answers "What was her dream?" and is the subject of "was", so it works as a noun. It has no subject of its own, so it is a phrase, not a clause.

q: Which sentence means that nobody except Hamza passed the test?
x: "Only" limits the word placed right next to it. Placed before "Hamza", it means no other person passed; placed near "test", it limits what Hamza passed.

q: Which sentence is free of a dangling modifier?
o: Walking to college, Ali saw a snake.
Walking to college, a snake was seen by Ali.
Walking to college, the snake frightened Ali.
While walking to college, a snake bit Ali.
x: An opening participle phrase must describe the subject that follows it. Only in the first sentence is the walker (Ali) the subject; the others make the snake the one walking to college.

q: Which of the following is a compound-complex sentence?
o: Bilal kept working because the report was urgent.
Bilal kept working, and his sister made him tea.
Although it was late, Bilal kept working, and his sister made him tea.
Despite the late hour, Bilal kept working.
x: A compound-complex sentence has at least two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause. The first sentence has two independent clauses joined by "and" plus the dependent clause "Although it was late".

q: Which sentence means that Fatima failed most of her subjects, but not all of them?
o: Fatima nearly failed in every subject.
x: Placed before "every subject", "almost" limits the number of subjects. Placed before the verb, as in "almost failed", it means she came close to failing but actually passed.

q: In "The man who sold us the car has moved to Karachi", the words "who sold us the car" form
x: The clause begins with the relative pronoun "who" and tells us which man, so it describes a noun and is an adjective (relative) clause. It cannot stand alone as a sentence.

q: In "I know that he is honest", the words "that he is honest" form
x: The clause answers "What do I know?" and is the object of the verb "know", so it works as a noun. It has its own subject and verb, so it is a clause, not a phrase.

q: Choose the correct option: "Never ___ such a beautiful sunset."
x: When a negative adverb such as "never" begins a sentence, the auxiliary verb comes before the subject: "Never have I seen".

q: Choose the correct word: "Hardly had the train left ___ it started raining."
x: "Hardly" is followed by "when" in this pattern. "Than" goes with "no sooner", not with "hardly".

q: Choose the correct word: "No sooner had the guests arrived ___ the lights went out."
x: "No sooner" contains the comparative "sooner", so it is completed by "than", not by "when".

q: Choose the correct option: "Only then ___ the seriousness of the situation."
x: A sentence that begins with "Only then" takes inversion with an auxiliary: "did" comes before the subject, and the main verb stays in its base form.

q: Which sentence is correct?
x: "Seldom" at the start requires inversion: "does" before the subject, followed by the base form "arrive". "Does Bilal arrives" wrongly marks the tense twice.

q: Which sentence has the same meaning as "If I had known about the test, I would have studied harder"?
o: Had I known about the test, I would have studied harder.
Did I know about the test, I would have studied harder.
Have I known about the test, I would have studied harder.
Had I know about the test, I would have studied harder.
x: In a third conditional, "if" can be dropped by moving "had" before the subject: "Had I known". The past participle "known" must stay.

q: Choose the correct option: "Not only ___ the exam, but she also won a scholarship."
x: When "Not only" begins a sentence, the first clause is inverted with an auxiliary: "Not only did she pass". The second clause keeps normal order.

q: Which sentence correctly rewrites "He had scarcely sat down when the phone rang" with inversion?
o: Scarcely he had sat down when the phone rang.
Scarcely had he sat down than the phone rang.
Scarcely had he sat down when the phone rang.
Scarcely did he sit down than the phone rang.
x: With "scarcely" first, "had" moves before the subject, and the pattern is completed by "when". "Than" belongs with "no sooner", not with "scarcely".

q: Which sentence beginning with "Under no circumstances" is correct?
o: Under no circumstances the records should be shared.
Under no circumstances should be the records shared.
Under no circumstances the records be shared should.
Under no circumstances should the records be shared.
x: A negative phrase such as "Under no circumstances" at the start causes inversion: only the auxiliary "should" moves before the subject "the records"; "be shared" stays after it.

q: Choose the correct option: "Little ___ that his friends were planning a surprise for him."
x: "Little" at the start, meaning "not at all", is negative, so it takes inversion with "did": "Little did Hamza know". Without inversion, "Little Hamza" would read as "the small boy Hamza".

q: Which sentence correctly uses inversion to express a condition?
o: Should you needed help, call me.
You should need help, call me.
Should need you help, call me.
Should you need help, call me.
x: "Should you need help" means "If you need help". "Should" comes before the subject and is followed by the base form "need".

q: Choose the passive form of "The teacher checks the copies."
o: The copies are checked by the teacher.
The copies were checked by the teacher.
The copies are being checked by the teacher.
The copies have been checked by the teacher.
x: The active verb is in the present simple, so the passive uses "are" + past participle: "are checked". The other options change the tense.

q: Choose the passive form of "Sara was writing a letter."
o: A letter was written by Sara.
A letter is being written by Sara.
A letter had been written by Sara.
A letter was being written by Sara.
x: The past continuous passive is "was/were being" + past participle. "Was written" drops the continuous sense, and "is being written" changes the tense to the present.

q: Choose the passive form of "Ali has repaired the fan."
o: The fan has been repaired by Ali.
The fan had been repaired by Ali.
The fan has repaired by Ali.
The fan was repaired by Ali.
x: The present perfect passive is "has/have been" + past participle. "Has repaired" without "been" is still active in form, and "had been" changes the tense to past perfect.

q: Choose the passive form of "You must finish this work."
o: This work must be finished by you.
This work must finish by you.
This work must have been finished by you.
This work must being finished by you.
x: With a modal, the passive is modal + "be" + past participle: "must be finished". "Must have been finished" refers to the past, which the active sentence does not.

q: Choose the passive form of "They will announce the results tomorrow."
o: The results would be announced by them tomorrow.
The results will be announced by them tomorrow.
The results will announce by them tomorrow.
The results will have been announced by them tomorrow.
x: The future simple passive is "will be" + past participle. "Will have been announced" is future perfect, and "will announce" is still active.

q: Choose the passive form of the command "Open the window."
x: An imperative is made passive with "Let" + object + "be" + past participle. After "let", the base form "be" is used, not "is".

q: Choose the passive form of "Did Hamza break the glass?"
o: Was the glass broken by Hamza?
Is the glass broken by Hamza?
Was the glass break by Hamza?
Had the glass been broken by Hamza?
x: A past simple question becomes "Was/Were" + subject + past participle. "Break" is not the past participle, and "is" and "had been" change the tense.

q: Choose the active form of "The patient is being examined by the doctor."
o: The doctor is examining the patient.
The doctor was examining the patient.
The doctor has examined the patient.
x: "Is being examined" is present continuous passive, so the active form is present continuous: "is examining". The other options change the tense.

q: Choose the passive form of "Who wrote this essay?"
o: By whom this essay was written?
By whom was this essay written?
By whom is this essay written?
x: "Who" as the doer becomes "By whom", and the past simple question takes "was" before the subject. Without that inversion it is not a question, and "is" changes the tense.

q: Which sentence is in the passive voice?
o: The workers built the bridge in 1990.
The bridge stood for thirty years.
The bridge collapsed in the flood.
x: In the passive the subject receives the action, and the verb is a form of "be" + past participle ("was built"). In the other sentences the subject does the action or the verb has no object.

q: Choose the correct passive form of "The principal gave Bilal a prize."
o: Bilal was gave a prize by the principal.
Bilal is given a prize by the principal.
Bilal was given a prize by the principal.
A prize was given Bilal to the principal.
x: Either object can become the subject; with "Bilal" as subject the past simple passive is "was given". "Gave" is not a past participle, "is given" changes the tense, and the last option reverses who gave to whom.

q: Choose the passive form of "Someone should have informed the police."
o: The police should had been informed.
The police should have been informed.
x: A modal perfect becomes modal + "have been" + past participle in the passive. "By someone" is usually left out because the doer is unknown. "Should be informed" loses the past meaning.

q: Choose the correct indirect form of: He said, "I was busy."
o: He said that I had been busy.
He said that he has been busy.
He told that he had been busy.
He said that he had been busy.
x: After a past reporting verb, the past simple "was" moves back to the past perfect "had been", and "I" becomes "he". "Told" must be followed by an object, such as "told me".

q: A week later, Bilal reports what Sara said: "I will visit Lahore tomorrow." Choose the correct indirect form.
o: Sara said that she would visit Lahore the next day.
Sara said that she will visit Lahore tomorrow.
Sara said that she would visit Lahore tomorrow.
Sara said that she would have visited Lahore the next day.
x: "Will" changes to "would", and since the report is made a week later, "tomorrow" becomes "the next day". "Would have visited" wrongly changes the meaning to something that did not happen.

q: Choose the correct indirect form of: Ali said to me, "Are you coming to the party?"
o: Ali asked me that was I coming to the party.
Ali asked me whether was I coming to the party.
Ali asked me if I was coming to the party.
Ali said me if I was coming to the party.
x: A yes/no question is reported with "asked" + "if/whether", and the question becomes normal statement order ("I was coming"). "That" is not used to report a question.

q: Choose the correct indirect form of: The teacher said to Hamza, "Where did you go yesterday?" (reported a few days later)
o: The teacher asked Hamza where he had gone the previous day.
The teacher asked Hamza where did he go the previous day.
The teacher asked Hamza where he had gone yesterday.
The teacher said to Hamza where he had gone the previous day.
x: A reported wh-question keeps the question word but uses statement order; the past simple moves back to past perfect, and "yesterday" becomes "the previous day". "Said to" is not used to report a question.

q: Choose the correct indirect form of: The doctor said to the patient, "Take this medicine twice a day."
o: The doctor told the patient to take that medicine twice a day.
The doctor told the patient that take this medicine twice a day.
The doctor told the patient to took that medicine twice a day.
The doctor said the patient to take that medicine twice a day.
x: A command is reported with a verb such as "told" + object + "to" + base form, and "this" usually becomes "that". "Said" cannot be followed directly by the listener as its object.

q: Choose the correct indirect form of: Mother said to us, "Don't play in the sun."
o: Mother told us not playing in the sun.
Mother told us don't play in the sun.
Mother told us not to play in the sun.
Mother told us that do not play in the sun.
x: A negative command is reported with "not to" + base form. The words "don't" and "do not" are not kept in indirect speech.

q: Choose the correct indirect form of: Ayesha said, "What a lovely garden!"
o: Ayesha exclaimed that what a lovely garden it was.
Ayesha exclaimed that it was a very lovely garden.
Ayesha exclaimed that it is a lovely garden what.
Ayesha said that what a lovely garden!
x: An exclamation is reported with a verb such as "exclaimed", and the exclamation becomes a statement with "very", in the past tense. "That" cannot be followed by the exclamatory "what a...".

q: A month later, Ali reports what Bilal said to him: "I met your brother yesterday." Choose the correct indirect form.
o: Bilal told Ali that he had met your brother the previous day.
Bilal told Ali that he has met Ali's brother yesterday.
Bilal told Ali that he had met Ali's brother the previous day.
Bilal told Ali that Ali had met his brother the previous day.
x: "I" (Bilal) becomes "he", "your" (Ali's) refers to the listener, "met" moves back to "had met", and "yesterday" becomes "the previous day". The last option reverses who met whom.

q: Choose the correct direct form of: Bilal said that he was feeling tired.
o: Bilal said, "I will be feeling tired."
x: Going back to direct speech, "he" (the speaker himself) becomes "I", and the past continuous "was feeling" returns to the present continuous "am feeling".

q: Choose the correct indirect form of: The teacher said, "The earth moves round the sun."
o: The teacher said that the earth moves round the sun.
The teacher said that the earth had moved round the sun.
The teacher said that the earth would move round the sun.
The teacher said that the earth has moved round the sun.
x: A universal truth keeps its present simple tense even after a past reporting verb. The other options wrongly suggest the fact was true only once or in the future.

q: Choose the correct indirect form of: Fatima said to Ali, "Please lend me your pen."
o: Fatima requested Ali to lend her his pen.
Fatima requested Ali to lend me your pen.
Fatima requested Ali that please lend her his pen.
Fatima said Ali to please lend her his pen.
x: A polite request is reported with "requested" + object + "to" + base form, and "please" is dropped. "Me" (Fatima) becomes "her" and "your" (Ali's) becomes "his".

q: Some years later, in another city, Sara reports what Hamza said: "I have lived here for ten years." Choose the correct indirect form.
o: Hamza said that he has lived there for ten years.
Hamza said that he had lived here for ten years.
Hamza said that he had lived there for ten years.
Hamza said that he was living here for ten years.
x: The present perfect "have lived" moves back to the past perfect "had lived". Since the report is made in a different place, "here" becomes "there".
